intro: This guide helps you lead twelve weekly sessions on Pandita Ramabai (For Children), the true story of a girl from India who was carried down a mountain in a cane box, lost her family in a famine, walked four thousand miles, came to know Jesus, and made a home for thousands of widows and orphan girls. It is best for children aged 8 to 12, and younger children can join in with a grown-up sitting close by. It works for a Sunday school class, a homeschool group or a family around the table.

Each session takes about thirty minutes. Welcome the children and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the week’s chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s short prayer, or one of your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand so nothing takes you by surprise, and have paper and crayons or pencils ready. Some chapters tell of famine, the deaths of Ramabai’s family and the unkind treatment of child widows, so read those parts calmly and simply, answer questions honestly without adding detail, never press anyone to share their own sad times in front of the group, and keep coming back to the book’s steady message that God held Ramabai in his hands all along. Ramabai grew up in a Hindu family who loved their holy books, so speak of India, its people and its faith with warmth and respect as you tell her story.

weeks.summary: Ramabai’s father, Anant Shastri, believes girls can learn the holy Sanskrit books too, so he takes his young wife Lakshmibai up a forest mountain to teach her; there, in April 1858, Ramabai is born. When his money runs out, baby Ramabai is carried down the mountain in a cane box on a man’s head, and later her mother teaches her long Sanskrit poems by heart while she picks up languages on the road. The big idea: God gives us parents and teachers, and learning is a good gift for girls and boys alike.

memory_verse.text: And you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

activity.title: Learn It by Heart
steps: Remind the children that Ramabai learned long poems by heart just by listening and saying them back.
Say the memory verse one short phrase at a time and have the group echo each phrase back to you.
Add a simple action for each phrase, such as sitting, walking on the spot, lying down and standing up.
Say the whole verse together with the actions, getting a little faster each time, then let a volunteer lead it once.

weeks.summary: Ramabai’s family travels for about fifteen years from one holy place to another, reading the old books aloud, and at Dwarka by the sea thousands wait to see a golden city that the story says will appear to people with no sin; Ramabai sees only ordinary clouds and knows it in her heart. She hears a young wife crying and first feels called to help girls and women, and her parents choose not to marry her as a little child so she can keep learning. The big idea: Jesus says the truth sets us free, and God gives us courage to be honest even when others keep quiet. Speak kindly of the people waiting on the shore; they were sincerely hoping, and the point is Ramabai’s honesty, not making fun of anyone.

memory_verse.text: You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.

activity.title: True or Not True?
steps: Have everyone stand in a space where they can crouch down.
Call out sentences, some true and some not, such as “Ramabai was born on a mountain,” “Ramabai was born in a busy city,” “Grass is purple,” or “God loves every child.”
Have the children stand tall for true and crouch down for not true.
Finish by saying the memory verse together, and talk about how it takes courage to stand up for what is true.

weeks.summary: When Ramabai is about sixteen, a famine comes to southern India; the family lose everything, and her blind old father gives her “into the hands of our God” before he dies, followed by her mother and her big sister. In the middle of it a kind neighbour gives Ramabai bread when she is too shy and sad to ask. The big idea: God does not call sad things good, but even when the people we love are gone, God does not leave us and holds us in his hands. This is the saddest chapter: read it slowly and gently, be aware that some children may have lost someone, and do not add any detail about hunger or dying beyond what the book says.

memory_verse.text: When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.

activity.title: Held in God’s Hands
steps: Have each child lay one hand flat on a sheet of paper and trace around it with a crayon.
Inside the hand, have them draw a small picture of themselves.
Help them write across the top, “God holds me in his hands.”
Let them keep their picture private, and pray together for children who are hungry or alone today.

weeks.summary: Ramabai and her brother Srinivas walk more than four thousand miles across India with no shoes or blankets, once keeping warm by covering themselves with sand beside a freezing river; Ramabai later says the hardship made her heart hard like a stone. In Calcutta in 1878 the scholars honour her as Pandita, “the learned lady,” and Christians give her a Sanskrit Bible she cannot yet understand but keeps all her life. The big idea: hard times can harden our hearts, but God loves to give us soft hearts that care about others. When the chapter mentions the old law books’ teaching about women, keep it to what Ramabai felt and speak respectfully of her people.

memory_verse.text: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.

activity.title: Stone Heart, Soft Heart
steps: Have each child fold a sheet of paper in half like a card.
On the front, have them draw a grey stone in the shape of a heart.
Inside, have them draw a big bright heart and fill it with small pictures or words of kind things a soft heart does, like sharing, helping or saying sorry.
Hold the cards up and open them together while you say the memory verse.

weeks.summary: Ramabai’s brother dies saying, “If God cares for us, I am afraid of nothing,” and she marries Bipin, has a baby girl named Manorama, “heart’s joy,” and finds the Gospel of Luke mysteriously on her bookshelf. Early in 1882 Bipin dies of cholera, leaving her a widow with a baby, yet she says her sadness drew her nearer to God. The big idea: when we are most alone, God is close and draws us to himself. Mention the deaths briefly and gently, and linger instead on the brave words of Srinivas and the joy of baby Manorama.

memory_verse.text: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, Is God in his holy habitation.

activity.title: Heart’s Joy Name Cards
steps: Remind the children that Manorama means “heart’s joy” and Pandita means “learned lady.”
Have each child write their own name in big letters across a sheet of paper and decorate it.
Help them write underneath, “God is near me,” and pass the cards round the circle.
As each card arrives, have the child holding it say one kind word about its owner, such as “friendly” or “brave,” then hand it back.

weeks.summary: In Poona, Ramabai starts a women’s club to help girls go to school and to help widows, and in 1882 she stands before British government visitors to ask for women teachers and women doctors, something hardly any Indian woman had done. When a twelve-year-old widow is brought to her, Ramabai takes her home, and a plan for a home for widows begins; in 1883 she sails for England “as Abraham, not knowing whither I went.” The big idea: God wants us to speak up for people who are hurt or left out. Explain child widows simply, as the book does, and do not act out how they were treated; keep the focus on Ramabai’s courage and kindness.

memory_verse.text: Open your mouth for the mute, In the cause of all who are left desolate.

activity.title: Who Needs a Voice?
steps: Sit in a circle and explain that you will describe some everyday moments where someone needs a friend to speak up.
Describe a child who is always picked last, a new child who does not speak the language yet, and someone who is being laughed at.
After each one, ask the group what kind and brave words they could say, and let a few children answer.
Choose one idea together to try this week, and say the memory verse to finish.

weeks.summary: In England the Sisters teach Ramabai English, but she learns she cannot train as a doctor because she is partly deaf. At a London home where Christians care for women others look down on, she asks why, and a Sister reads her John 4, where Jesus talks kindly with the woman at the well and offers living water; Ramabai becomes sure Jesus is the Saviour, and on 29 September 1883 she and Manorama are baptised. The big idea: Jesus never looks down on anyone and offers his living water to everyone. If children ask about the women in the London home, simply say their lives had gone wrong and people looked down on them, as the book does.

memory_verse.text: But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.

activity.title: Pass the Living Water
steps: Sit in a circle and pretend to hold a cup of cool water in your hands.
Pass the pretend cup carefully to the child beside you and say one kind thing to them as you give it.
Have each child do the same, passing the cup round the circle with a kind word, until everyone has been given one.
Remind them that Jesus’ living water never runs out, then say the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: Ramabai spends nearly three years in America, writes a book about the women of India, and on 11 March 1889 opens Sharada Sadan, “the Home of Wisdom,” a school for young widows that starts with just two pupils and grows. She promises not to make the girls Christians, but she reads the Bible and prays each morning with her door open, and one by one girls come in because they want to. The big idea: we need not be pushy about Jesus or hide him either; we can leave the door open by being kind and honest. Speak respectfully of the Hindu advisers and of the girls’ own faith, as Ramabai did.

memory_verse.text: Learn to do well; seek justice, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.

activity.title: The Open Door
steps: Have each child fold the two sides of a sheet of paper in to meet in the middle, making two doors that open.
On the front of the doors, have them draw a door handle and decorate the doors.
Open the doors and, inside, have them draw a happy room where friends are welcome, perhaps with people singing together like Ramabai’s girls.
Open the doors together and say the memory verse, then sing a song the group knows well.

weeks.summary: Ramabai starts reading the Bible itself every day and sees that she needs “Christ, and not merely His religion”; about 1891 she gives herself completely to Jesus and feels a heavy load roll off her heart, rejoicing that God’s love is a free gift, “for me, a woman!” In 1893 helpers leave in anger, families take their daughters away and some people even threaten her, but she trusts God and comes through braver. The big idea: Jesus wants us not just to know about him but to know and trust him ourselves. Mention the threats only briefly and stress that God set her free from fear.

memory_verse.text: The people who sat in darkness saw a great light, to those who sat in the region and shadow of death, to them did light spring up.

activity.title: The Load Rolls Away
activity.materials: One sheet of scrap paper per child, pencils, and one large sheet with a cross drawn on it
steps: Lay the large sheet with the cross on the floor in the middle of the room.
Give each child a scrap of paper and invite them, privately, to scribble or draw something heavy they would like to give to Jesus; no one will look at it.
Have them crumple their paper into a ball, a little heavy load.
One at a time, let them gently roll their ball onto the cross, then gather the balls up and throw them away unopened while you all say, “Thank you, Jesus!”

weeks.summary: When famine comes again in 1896, Ramabai hears God say, “Remember the days of old,” remembers her own hungry childhood, and goes to rescue girls with no food or family, trusting that “the Lord knows what I need.” On the way home she leaves behind a girl who had taken beans and run away, then stops the carts, remembers how God loved her while she was still a sinner, and waves Girija back. The big idea: God loves us first, before we are good, and helps us forgive and welcome others. The book mentions people who wanted to steal girls away and hurt them; read it as written and do not expand on it.

memory_verse.text: But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, christ died for us.

activity.title: Waved Back Home
steps: Have each child draw a line of bullock carts by a river, with Ramabai standing up in the front cart waving.
Have them draw Girija running towards the carts as fast as she can, with a big smile.
Help them write across the top, “God loves me first.”
Hold up the pictures, everyone give a big wave like Ramabai, and say the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: Moved out of Poona by the plague in 1897, Ramabai takes her girls to a farm at Kedgaon and names it Mukti, “being set free”; like George Müller she trusts God for everything with no bank account, and by 1901 about two thousand women and girls live there, learning to read, farm, weave and print. Though honoured as a learned lady, she calls herself a sweeper: “I sweep into this compound as many as I can get.” The big idea: we can trust God with our needs and welcome people others leave out.

memory_verse.text: My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

activity.title: Sweep Everyone In
steps: Have the children spread out around the room and choose one child to be Ramabai the sweeper.
The sweeper walks to any child, takes their hand and says, “Come in, you are welcome!”
Now both walk together to gather another child, and the line keeps growing, always walking and never running.
When everyone has been swept in, stand in one big circle and say the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: In 1905 hundreds of girls at Mukti pray, and God answers with sorrow for wrongdoing, joy and love, which Ramabai calls the most important sign of God’s Spirit. She learns Hebrew and Greek to give her people a Bible in simple everyday Marathi, printed by the girls and never sold; her daughter Manorama dies in 1921, and Ramabai dies quietly in her sleep in 1922, with a thousand girls following her coffin and Mukti still caring for women and children today. The big idea: Ramabai was given God’s love freely, so she gave it freely; mention the two deaths gently, and this is a good week to look back over the whole story.

memory_verse.text: Freely you received, so freely give.

activity.title: A Verse to Give Away
steps: Have each child fold a sheet of paper in half and then in half again to make a little booklet.
On the cover, help them write “Given freely” and draw a picture from Ramabai’s story they remember.
Inside, have them copy their favourite memory verse from these twelve weeks in their own simple words, just as Ramabai made the Bible easy to understand.
Invite them to give the booklet away this week to someone, and pray for that person together.
